lessons.title: Why seed moisture matters and preparing the work area
lessons.html:
Why seed moisture matters and preparing the work area

Moisture content is the amount of water in the seed, given as a percentage of the seed's weight. It is one of the most important things to know about a seed lot. Seed that is too wet heats up, grows fungi, attracts insects and loses germination quickly in storage. Seed that is dried too hard can crack during processing. Processing plants use moisture results to decide whether to dry seed, and storage managers use them to judge how long a lot can be kept.

Methods

  • Oven method: the reference method. A weighed sample is dried in an oven, and the weight lost is the water. The testing rules your laboratory follows (usually ISTA rules) set the temperature, time and whether the seed must be ground first for each crop.
  • Moisture meters: quick electronic meters used at intake and in the plant. They must be checked against the oven method regularly.

Preparing the work area

  • Clean the bench, grinder and containers. Old seed or flour in a grinder changes the result.
  • Check that the oven is at the set temperature with a calibrated thermometer, and that temperature records are kept.
  • Check the analytical balance with test weights and make sure it is level and out of draughts.
  • Prepare clean, dry, labelled containers with lids, and a desiccator with active desiccant for cooling.

Safety

Ovens and containers are hot: use tongs or heat-resistant gloves. Grinders have sharp moving parts; switch off and unplug before cleaning. Treated seed must be handled with gloves, and grinding treated seed creates dust, so use dust extraction or a mask if your procedure requires it.

lessons.title: Preparing the moisture sample and documentation
lessons.html:
Preparing the moisture sample and documentation

The biggest risk in a moisture test is that the sample gains or loses water before you weigh it. A sample left open on the bench on a dry Highveld winter day can lose moisture; one left in a humid room can gain moisture. Work quickly and keep samples sealed.

The submitted sample

  • Moisture samples must arrive in moisture-proof, sealed containers or bags. If a sample arrives in a paper bag, it may not be suitable; report it according to procedure.
  • Check the sample number, crop and request on the submission form.
  • Let a cold sample reach room temperature while still sealed, so moisture does not condense on it.

Preparing the working sample

  1. Mix the sample well inside its container.
  2. Take the working sample quickly, by spoon or divider, as the rules say. Remove obvious foreign matter such as stones if the method requires.
  3. Grind the seed if the crop requires it, to the fineness in the method. Work fast and do not let the ground seed stand open.
  4. Do duplicate determinations, as the rules usually require two independent samples.

Documentation

Record for each determination:

ItemExample
Sample numberFrom the submission form
Container numberMarked on the container and lid
M1: empty container and lidWeighed
M2: container, lid and sample before dryingWeighed
Oven start time and temperatureFrom the oven

Weigh to the number of decimal places required by the method. Handle containers with tongs or gloves; fingerprints and moisture from your hands add weight.

lessons.title: Completing the moisture determination
lessons.html:
Completing the moisture determination

After the drying time set in the method, the samples are removed, cooled and weighed again.

Drying and cooling

  1. Place the open containers, with lids beside or under them, in the oven at the correct temperature. Start timing when the oven returns to temperature.
  2. At the end of the drying time, close the lids quickly and move containers to the desiccator using tongs.
  3. Let them cool to room temperature in the desiccator. Warm containers weigh wrongly on the balance.
  4. Weigh each container with its lid and dried sample. This is M3.

Calculation

Moisture content (%) = (M2 minus M3) divided by (M2 minus M1), multiplied by 100.

Example: M1 = 20.000 g, M2 = 25.000 g, M3 = 24.400 g. Water lost = 0.600 g. Sample weight = 5.000 g. Moisture = 0.600 / 5.000 x 100 = 12.0%.

Checking results

  • Calculate both duplicates. If they differ by more than the tolerance in the testing rules, repeat the test.
  • Report the average, rounded as the rules require.
  • Compare with storage and processing limits used by the company and flag high-moisture lots to the supervisor at once, because they may need drying.

Completing the process

  • Complete and sign the worksheet and pass it on for checking.
  • Discard dried seed according to procedure; treated seed goes to hazardous waste.
  • Clean containers, grinder and bench. Regenerate or replace desiccant when its indicator shows it is spent.
  • Record and report any equipment problem, such as an oven that did not hold its temperature.

Key points

  • Seed that is too wet heats, moulds and loses germination in storage.
  • The oven method is the reference; meters are checked against it.
  • Keep samples sealed and work quickly so moisture does not change.
  • Cool samples in a desiccator before weighing.
  • Moisture % = (M2 - M3) / (M2 - M1) x 100; duplicates must agree.
